neighbours.label: the end of the first item after 'neither' (or Spanish/French 'ni', German 'weder'), where 'nor' / 'ni' / 'noch' is due next; quiet after 'either' and 'both', where 'or' / 'and' is due
fire: The report found that neither the pilot nor the ground crew had been warned about the storm.
In the end neither her parents, nor her teachers, nor her friends could change her mind.
He owned neither land nor cattle when he arrived in the colony.
The publisher states that neither the author nor the editors are liable for any errors.
It turned out that neither the old bridge, nor the ferry could carry the heavy trucks.
The soup was neither hot nor properly seasoned, so we sent it back.
The court held that neither the tenant nor the landlord had kept a copy of the lease.
She trusted neither the doctors, nor the pills they kept giving her.
quiet: The report found that either the pilot or the ground crew had been warned about the storm.
In the end both her parents, and her teachers, and her friends tried to change her mind.
He owned both land and cattle when he arrived in the colony.
The publisher states that the author and the editors are liable for any errors.
It turned out that either the old bridge, or the ferry could carry the heavy trucks.
The soup was not only hot but properly seasoned, so we ordered more.
The court held that both the tenant and the landlord had kept a copy of the lease.
She trusted the doctors, and the pills they kept giving her.

notes: Card: top examples in Spanish, German, French and English all sit on the last token of the first conjunct after ni / weder / neither; output promotes ' ni', ' noch' and suppresses ' or', ' both'. Probes: 'Neither the manager,' 0.49, 'Neither the hotel' 0.37, 'neither money' 0.60, Spanish 0.17; 'Either the manager,' 0.01, 'Both the manager,' 0.00. Near misses swap in either / both / not only with the same nouns.
